To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adoptively transferred CD8 T cells do not control SIV replication in vivo, and that CD8 T cells with a partially activated phenotype persist in the lungs without dividing.

1) adoptive transfer of SIV-specific CD4+ or CD8+ TCR transgenic T cell lines or in vitro expanded CD8+ T-cell clones did not appreciibly impact acute or chronic viremia, 2) allogeneic SIV-specific CD3+ T cells were not detected after 3 d in the blood or in most tissues, 3) allogeneically transferred SIV-specific CD5+ T cells persisted longer in the lung than

adoptive transfer of allogeneic or autologous CD8+ T-cell clones specific for a single epitope of the SIVmac239 Gag protein into rhesus monkeys infected with SIVmac239 does not impact acute or chronic SIV replication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of CD8 T cells in controlling viral replication in HIV/SIV-infected rhesus macaque models.
understanding how CD8+ T-cell immunity is generated and how it can be manipulated to control HIV/SIV infection.
the study of the mechanisms of immune evasion and immune escape by the virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CD8+ T-cell response is a critical component of the host defense against HIV, but that it is not sufficient to control the disease in the absence of additional immune responses.
the adoptive transfer of CD8+ cells does not control SIV replication in vivo, and this is likely to be true in the context of HIV as well.
the transfer of CD8+ cells is not sufficient for control of SIV replication.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adoptively transferred CD8+ T-cell clones did not impact the viral replication.
adoptive transfer of SIV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell clones did not control SIV replication in rhesus macaque models.
CD8+ T lymphocytes are not sufficient for the control of SIV replication.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of Ag-specific CD8 T cells needed to limit viral replication is very high.
the magnitude of the CD8+ T-cell response required to control SIV replication is much larger than that which is achievable with adoptive transfer of in vitro-expanded CD8+ T clones.

adoptive transfer of large numbers of SIV-specific CD4+ T cell clones is a feasible approach in macaques and can be used to test the ability of CD4+ T cells to limit viral replication in the absence or presence of CD8+ responses.
